274.title: "A clear victory"
274.hook: the treaty is called a clear victory, and peace lets the call of Islam spread (48:1)
274.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite Surah al-Fath in times of hope, and teachers point to Hudaybiyyah when counseling patience with setbacks and trust that a loss may be an opening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the treaty at Hudaybiyyah, a peace that hurt. Your line was it looked like losing. What did you let go of for the sake of peace? Day two hundred seventy-four.

The pilgrims are riding home to Medina, heads shaved, no pilgrimage done, and the mood is heavy. Umar can't let it go. He rides up beside the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and asks him something, and gets no answer. He asks again. No answer. A third time. Nothing. Umar drops back, sure he's gone too far, afraid a verse is about to come down about him. Then someone calls his name: the Prophet wants you. Umar rides up, braced for the worst. And the Prophet says, as Sahih al-Bukhari tells it: tonight a surah has come to me that is dearer to me than everything the sun rises on. Today: a clear victory.
screen: `RIDING HOME, HEADS SHAVED.` → `UMAR ASKS THREE TIMES.` → `DEARER THAN ALL THE SUN RISES ON.`

segments.voice: The surah is al-Fath, the Victory, Surah 48. And it opens: we have given you a clear victory, fathan mubina. Fath means an opening, and a victory. It's the same root as al-Fattah, the Opener, one of the names we met a few weeks ago. Umar, in another report, asks the obvious thing: messenger of God, is this a victory? And the Prophet says: yes. Everyone could see what had been lost. What the surah saw was what had been opened. Here's how it played out. With the roads at peace, people could travel between Mecca and Medina without fear. They talked. They traded. Families on both sides met again. And they heard the Qur'an, not over the noise of war, but in ordinary conversation. The early scholar az-Zuhri, as Ibn Ishaq reports him, said there was no greater victory in Islam before it: in the two years after Hudaybiyyah, as many people became Muslim as in all the years before, or more. Ibn Hisham, who edited Ibn Ishaq's book, pointed to the numbers: about fourteen hundred came to Hudaybiyyah, and two years later, ten thousand marched to Mecca. Two of Mecca's commanders, Khalid ibn al-Walid, the man who turned the battle at Uhud, and 'Amr ibn al-'As, both came to Medina during the peace and became Muslim. Even the clause that hurt most, sending back those who fled Mecca, was dropped by the Meccans themselves not long after, when it started to cost them more than it cost the Muslims. The Qur'an says elsewhere that you may dislike something that is good for you. Hudaybiyyah is often told to show what that line means.
screen: `FATH — AN OPENING, A VICTORY.` · `IS THIS A VICTORY? YES.` · `FOURTEEN HUNDRED, THEN TEN THOUSAND.` · `YOU MAY DISLIKE WHAT IS GOOD.` · then, large: `LOSING, THEN WINNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look again at a setback. Sit, and bring back something from your past that felt like a clear loss at the time. The rejection. The breakup. The plan that fell apart. Stay with how it felt then. Now look at what it opened. What came into your life through the gap it left? It may be nothing yet. That's allowed. Just look, with the question Umar asked: is this a victory? The bell holds the time.
A clear victory. Fathan mubina: what the Qur'an called the treaty everyone thought was a loss, the peace that opened the way. Today's word.
Your line: losing, then winning. Today, when something goes against you, say to yourself: it's too early to call it. Day two hundred seventy-four.

275.title: Letters to kings
275.hook: letters go to Heraclius, the Persian king, the Negus and others
275.howItsDone: Muslims read the letters and the Heraclius hadith, found in the opening book of Sahih al-Bukhari, as a model of respectful, direct invitation, and some Muslim men wear a ring on the little finger following the Prophet's seal ring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a clear victory, the treaty that opened the way. Your line was losing, then winning. Did something go against you that might still turn? Day two hundred seventy-five.

Mud-brick houses. A mosque roofed with palm leaves. From this small town, Medina, riders set out with letters. One is heading for the emperor of Rome. One for the king of kings of Persia. One for the Christian king of Abyssinia. One for the ruler of Egypt. Two of them rule the great empires of the day. It's a little like a small-town mayor writing personally to the heads of the world's great powers. But somebody in Medina points out a problem: kings don't read letters unless they're sealed. So the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has a ring made. Today: letters to kings.
screen: `A TOWN OF MUD BRICK.` → `LETTERS TO EMPERORS.` → `KINGS ONLY READ SEALED LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari describes the ring: silver, engraved with three words in three lines. Muhammad. Messenger. God. The letters went out in the calm after Hudaybiyyah, when the roads were safe. The one to the Roman emperor, kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, has this shape: in the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate; from Muhammad, the servant of God and his messenger, to the great one of his people; peace on whoever follows guidance. Then an invitation to Islam, and a verse from the Qur'an calling the People of the Book to a word common between them: that we worship none but God. The emperor, Heraclius, was in Jerusalem. And Bukhari keeps an account of what he did. He called for anyone from Arabia who happened to be nearby, and found a trading caravan from Mecca, traveling because of the new peace, led by Abu Sufyan, still the Prophet's enemy. Heraclius questioned him closely. Does this man lie? No. Does he break promises? No. Who follows him, the powerful or the weak? The weak. Abu Sufyan said later he wanted to lie, but was ashamed to be caught lying in front of his own men. The emperor treated the letter with respect, and in the end kept his throne and his faith. The king of Persia tore his letter to pieces. The biographers say the Negus of Abyssinia received his kindly, and the ruler of Egypt sent back courteous words and gifts. Different kings, different answers. The letters were the same: honest, short, sealed, and sent.
screen: `MUHAMMAD. MESSENGER. GOD.` · `PEACE ON WHOEVER FOLLOWS GUIDANCE.` · `HERACLIUS QUESTIONS ABU SUFYAN.` · `DIFFERENT KINGS, DIFFERENT ANSWERS.` · then, large: `SEALED AND SENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one honest letter. Not to a king. To someone you've been meaning to say something true to. A thank-you you never sent. An apology. A word of support. Sit, and let the person come to mind. Then draft it in your head, short, like the Prophet's letters: who it's from, who it's to, peace, and one honest thing. Don't decide yet whether you'll send it. Just write it. The bell holds the time.
Letters to kings. The sealed letters the Prophet sent from Medina to the emperor of Rome, the king of Persia, the Negus and others. Today's word.
Your line: sealed and sent. Today, send the letter you wrote in your head, a text, a card, an email, whatever reaches them. Day two hundred seventy-five.

276.title: Khaybar and Safiyyah
276.hook: after Khaybar, Safiyyah, daughter of a Jewish chief, becomes his wife and a mother of the believers
276.howItsDone: Muslims honor the Prophet's wives as mothers of the believers, following 33:6, and Safiyyah bint Huyayy is often remembered through the hadith of 'my father is Aaron, my uncle is Moses'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, letters to kings, honest and short. Your line was sealed and sent. Did you send the letter you wrote in your head? Day two hundred seventy-six.

Some people's lives turn completely in a single week. Safiyyah's did. She was the daughter of Huyayy, a chief of the Jewish tribe of Banu an-Nadir, a young woman from one of the most respected families of the old Jewish communities of Arabia. Her people had once lived in Medina, and been expelled after conflict with the Muslims, and settled in Khaybar, a rich oasis of date palms and stone forts north of the city. Some of their leaders had helped rally the great army at the Trench. In the seventh year after the migration, the Muslims marched on Khaybar. When it was over, her husband was dead, and she was a captive. Today: Khaybar and Safiyyah.
screen: `A CHIEF'S DAUGHTER.` → `AN OASIS OF FORTS.` → `ONE WEEK, EVERYTHING CHANGES.`

segments.voice: The Muslim sources tell what happened next briefly. Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ freed Safiyyah and married her, and made her freedom her dowry. An early biographer, Ibn Sa'd, adds that he gave her a choice: to go free, back to her people, or to become Muslim and marry him, and that she chose him. The sources say much less about what she felt that week, and it's honest to say so. Modern readers, Muslim and not, have asked hard questions about a marriage made in the aftermath of a battle, and Muslim scholars have answered with what the sources report of her choice and of the marriage that followed. What the sources do keep are small, clear moments. Bukhari says that when they set out, the Prophet sat down by his camel and put out his knee, and Safiyyah stepped on his knee to mount. And at-Tirmidhi keeps a hadith from later on. Some of the other wives teased her, calling her the daughter of a Jew, and she came to the Prophet in tears. He told her: say to them, my father is Aaron, my uncle is Moses, and my husband is Muhammad. What do you have over me? He didn't ask her to hide where she came from. He told her it was a lineage of prophets, Muslims' prophets too. Safiyyah lived for decades after him, known for her generosity and her good sense. The Qur'an calls the Prophet's wives mothers of the believers, and she is one of them: a woman from Khaybar, honored by her full name, and by her family.
screen: `FREED, AND HER FREEDOM HER DOWRY.` · `THE SOURCES SAY LITTLE OF HER HEART.` · `SHE STEPPED ON HIS KNEE.` · `MY FATHER IS AARON.` · then, large: `A MOTHER OF BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone from a different background. Sit, and think of someone in your life whose family, faith, country or language is different from yours. Maybe someone who's been teased for it, or made to feel it. Think about what their background has given them, and given you through them. Then picture one way you could honor it: asking about it, remembering a holiday, saying their name the way they say it. The bell holds the time.
Khaybar and Safiyyah. The oasis the Muslims took in the seventh year, and the chief's daughter who became the Prophet's wife and a mother of the believers. Today's word.
Your line: a mother of believers. Today, do the one thing you pictured to honor someone's background, and let it be sincere. Day two hundred seventy-six.

277.title: The conquest of Mecca
277.hook: the Prophet ﷺ enters Mecca with ten thousand, almost without fighting, head bowed
277.howItsDone: Muslims remember the conquest of Mecca, in Ramadan, as the moment the Kaaba was cleared of idols and returned to the worship of one God, and it's often told as a lesson in humility and mercy in victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khaybar and Safiyyah, a chief's daughter honored for her family. Your line was a mother of believers. Did you honor someone's background today? Day two hundred seventy-seven.

Years ago, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ slipped out of Mecca by night, hunted, with a price on his head. He looked back at the city and said he loved it, and would never have left if its people hadn't driven him out. Now it's Ramadan again. Mecca's allies have broken the peace of Hudaybiyyah, attacking a tribe allied to the Muslims. And one night the people of Mecca look out from the hills and see the valley below covered in campfires. The army behind them is ten thousand strong. The man they drove out has come back. Everyone in the city knows what conquerors do. Today: the conquest of Mecca.
screen: `YEARS AGO, BY NIGHT.` → `THE PEACE IS BROKEN.` → `TEN THOUSAND CAMPFIRES.`

segments.voice: That night, Abu Sufyan, Mecca's leader and the Prophet's old enemy, came out to see the camp, and before the army entered he had become Muslim. Sahih al-Bukhari says he was made to stand at a narrow pass and watch the army file by, tribe after tribe, until the Prophet's own company came past. And the Prophet sent him back to the city with an offer, recorded in Sahih Muslim: whoever enters Abu Sufyan's house is safe. Whoever shuts his own door is safe. Whoever enters the Sacred Mosque is safe. In other words: stay home, and nothing will happen to you. As the columns moved in, one commander, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, called out that today was the day of slaughter. Bukhari says the Prophet answered that Sa'd had it wrong: this is a day on which God will honor the Kaaba. The early biographers add that he took the banner from Sa'd, and they remember the reply as: today is the day of mercy. There was a brief clash on one side of the city. Otherwise, Mecca was entered almost without a fight. And the Prophet himself? The biographers describe him riding in on his camel with his head bowed so low, in humility before God, that his beard nearly touched the saddle. A companion in Sahih al-Bukhari remembered him reciting Surah al-Fath, the Victory, as he rode, softly, his voice wavering over the sounds. The surah that came after Hudaybiyyah, when it all looked like losing. He had left this city hunted, at night. He came back with its gates open, and he came back bowing.
screen: `ABU SUFYAN WATCHES THE ARMY PASS.` · `WHOEVER SHUTS HIS DOOR IS SAFE.` · `A DAY TO HONOR THE KAABA.` · `HEAD BOWED, RECITING AL-FATH.` · then, large: `HEAD BOWED ON THE CAMEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enter a room humbly. Sit, and picture the next room you'll walk into where you have some standing: your team, your family, a class you teach, a place where people wait on your word. Picture yourself walking in the way the Prophet rode into Mecca: head a little lowered, voice soft, not taking up more space than you need. If you pray, you can remember that every win is God's. The bell holds the time.
The conquest of Mecca. The Prophet's return to the city that drove him out, with ten thousand, almost without fighting, and his head bowed. Today's word.
Your line: head bowed on the camel. Today, when you get something you wanted, receive it quietly, with your head a little lower. Day two hundred seventy-seven.

278.title: "Go, you are free"
278.hook: he forgives the people who drove him out, echoing Yusuf, no blame on you today (12:92)
278.howItsDone: Muslims retell the forgiveness at the conquest of Mecca as a model of mercy, and many teachers use it, together with Yusuf's words to his brothers, when urging people to forgive relatives and old enemies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the conquest of Mecca: ten thousand at his back, and the Prophet ﷺ riding in with his head bowed so low his beard nearly touched the saddle. Your line was head bowed on the camel. Did you walk into a room a little more quietly? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

The square around the Ka'ba is full that day, and the faces are familiar. Some of these people had mocked him in the street for years. Some had boycotted his clan, shutting them up hungry in a narrow valley, chased him out of his hometown, and fought him at Badr and Uhud. One of the women in that crowd had rejoiced over the body of his uncle Hamzah. Now the city is his. There's no army left to stop him. The early biographies say he turned to them and asked a question: what do you think I'm going to do to you? And they answered carefully, the way you answer when your life depends on it: good. You're a noble brother, the son of a noble brother. Today, what he said next.
screen: `THE PEOPLE WHO DROVE HIM OUT.` → `WHAT DO YOU THINK I'LL DO?` → `GOOD, NOBLE BROTHER.`

segments.voice: According to the early accounts of his life, he said: I say to you what Yusuf said to his brothers. No blame on you today. Go, you are free. Hold on to that first sentence, because he didn't make up a speech. He reached for a story everyone listening knew. In the Qur'an's twelfth surah, Joseph's brothers throw him into a well, and he is sold away. Years later they stand in front of him in Egypt, hungry, not knowing who he is, and when they finally realize, they're ashamed. And Yusuf says, in the Qur'an's words, that there is no blame on them this day, and that God will forgive them. The Prophet stepped into that story on purpose. He was saying: you're my brothers, and I'm doing what Yusuf did. The word the reports use for the people of Mecca after this is tulaqa', the freed ones. The ones who were let go. Notice what forgiveness here is not. It isn't pretending nothing happened. Everyone in that square knew exactly what had happened; that's why they were afraid. It isn't weakness either. He could have done anything. It's choosing, from a position of strength, not to collect the debt. Some of the people let go that day became Muslims, and some later became leaders of the community. Muslim teachers often point out that he wasn't only forgiving strangers. Some of these people were his own relatives. Family is often the hardest place to say: go, you're free.
screen: `WHAT YUSUF SAID TO HIS BROTHERS.` · `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.` · `TULAQA' — THE FREED ONES.` · `FORGIVING FROM STRENGTH.` · then, large: `GO, YOU ARE FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive an old enemy in your heart. Sit, and let your breath slow. Think of someone who hurt you a long time ago. Not the worst thing that ever happened to you; something you've been carrying for a while. You don't have to call them. You don't have to say it was fine. Just picture them for a moment, and see if you can let the debt go, even a little. If you pray, you can ask God to forgive them, and you. If you don't, just try the words quietly: go, you're free. The bell holds the time.
Go. The first word of what he told the people who'd driven him out: go, you are free. Today's word.

Your line: go, you are free. Today, when an old grudge surfaces, in traffic, at a family dinner, scrolling past a name, say the line once to yourself and see what it loosens. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

279.title: Idols from the House
279.hook: the idols are removed from the Ka'ba as he recites, truth has come and falsehood vanished (17:81)
279.howItsDone: Muslims recite 17:81 when speaking of the conquest of Mecca and the clearing of the Ka'ba, and teachers use the scene to explain tawhid: the house restored to the worship of one God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people who had driven him out waited for his answer, and he gave them Yusuf's words: no blame on you today. Go, you are free. Did an old grudge loosen at all? Day two hundred seventy-nine.

The Ka'ba is a plain stone house in a valley, which the Qur'an says Abraham and his son Ishmael raised for the worship of the one God. On the day of the conquest, idols stand around it, three hundred and sixty of them, Sahih al-Bukhari says. Stone and wood, gods of many names. For generations, pilgrims had come to this house and prayed to them. The Prophet ﷺ walks up to them with a stick in his hand. Nobody fights him. Nobody stops him. He's reciting something as he goes, and the words are older than this morning. Today, the house gets cleared.
screen: `A HOUSE ABRAHAM RAISED.` → `THREE HUNDRED AND SIXTY IDOLS.` → `A STICK, AND A VERSE.`

segments.voice: Sahih al-Bukhari records the scene. As he went round the idols, he pointed at them with the stick, or struck them, and they fell, and he recited a verse from the seventeenth surah. In Pickthall's old translation it reads: "Truth hath come and falsehood hath vanished away. Lo! falsehood is ever bound to vanish." Look at the way that verse is built. It doesn't say truth fought falsehood and won after a long war. It says truth came, and falsehood simply went. Like turning on a light: you don't have to drag the dark out of the room. Muslims read the clearing of the Ka'ba as a return, not a new building. In their telling, the house was always meant for one God, and the idols were the add-ons, piled up over time. So removing them was a kind of restoration, the house given back to what it was for. The reports add a detail: images inside the Ka'ba were removed too, and he would not enter until they were. And notice what did not happen. The people who had prayed to those idols were the same people he set free that same day. The statues came down. The people were let go. Muslim teachers often hold those two side by side: firm about the false thing, gentle with the person who held it. That's a hard balance in any family argument. And look at the verse's last line: falsehood is ever bound to vanish. Muslims read it as a rule, not a single morning.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear one false thing from your room. Sit first, and look around. Is there something in your space that tells you a lie? A mirror you only use to criticize yourself. A screen that promises rest and never gives it. A note you keep that says you're not enough. Just notice it, and decide what you'll do with it after the bell. If you pray, you can recite the verse quietly, as he recited it: truth has come. If you don't, just sit with the room a little clearer. The bell holds the time.

280.title: Bilal on the roof
280.hook: the once-enslaved Bilal climbs the Ka'ba to call the adhan
280.howItsDone: Muslims honor Bilal as the first muezzin, and the adhan he called is still sung from mosques five times a day; his story is often told to teach that nobility lies in conduct, not birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, idols from the House: the statues fell as he recited, truth has come, and falsehood vanished away. Did you clear one false thing from your room? Day two hundred eighty, the end of the week.

Who gets the best seat at the celebration? At most victory parties it's the generals, the donors, the old families. On the day Mecca opened, the early biographies say the Prophet ﷺ turned to one man and told him to climb up onto the roof of the Ka'ba and call the prayer. Not a chief of Quraysh. Not one of his own relatives. Bilal: a Black man from Abyssinian stock, born enslaved, in this very city. Some of the Meccan nobles standing below watched him go up, and the reports say a few of them muttered about it. Then his voice went out over the valley. Today, the man on the roof.
screen: `WHO GETS THE BEST SEAT?` → `CLIMB UP AND CALL.` → `BILAL, BORN ENSLAVED.`

segments.voice: To feel what that moment meant, go back to the early years in Mecca. Bilal was an early Muslim, and he belonged to a man named Umayya, one of the Prophet's fiercest enemies. The biographies say Umayya would drag him out into the midday heat of Mecca, lay him on the burning ground, and put a heavy rock on his chest, demanding he give up the one God. And Bilal would only say one word, over and over: ahad, ahad. One. One. Abu Bakr bought him and set him free. In Medina, Bilal's strong voice made him the first mu'adhdhin, the one who calls the adhan, five times a day. Now it's the conquest. The same streets. The same people, some of them. And the man they had crushed under a rock is standing on the roof of the Ka'ba, calling: God is greatest. The Qur'an puts the principle in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Not the richest, not the best born. Bilal on the roof made that verse visible. Muslims still honor him; mosques and children carry his name, and the muezzin's role is often traced back to him. And this whole week has been one arc: a treaty that looked like losing, letters sealed and sent to kings, Safiyyah becoming a mother of believers, a head bowed on the camel, go, you are free, truth has come. And, at the top of it, Bilal.
screen: `AHAD, AHAD — ONE, ONE.` · `THE FIRST MU'ADHDHIN.` · `THE NOBLEST IS THE BEST IN CONDUCT.` · `THIS WEEK: A VICTORY WITHOUT REVENGE.` · then, large: `BILAL ON TOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone once looked down on. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of someone around you who usually gets overlooked. The quiet one on the team. The person who cleans the building. The relative who never gets asked for an opinion. Picture them for a moment in the place of honor, and ask yourself what one small thing you could do today to put them there: ask their advice, say their name with thanks, give them the good seat. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Bilal on the roof. The once-enslaved caller of the prayer, lifted to the top of the Ka'ba on the day Mecca opened. Today's word.
Your line: bilal on top. Today, give the best seat, the first word or the credit to someone who doesn't usually get it. Day two hundred eighty.
